responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response: Red. No matter what the majority does, pressing red guarantees your survival: if blue wins, everyone (including you) survives; if red wins, only red pressers survive. Blue adds unnecessary risk. The only case for blue is if you assume perfect coordination by everyone, but absent that, red is strictly safer.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer: Red.

Why red
- Dominance reasoning: For any pattern of others’ choices:
  - If blue is the majority, everyone survives, including you whether you pressed red or blue.
  - If red is the majority, only red pressers survive.
  So pressing red never makes you worse off and sometimes makes you better off. It weakly dominates blue and guarantees survival regardless of the outcome.

Steelmanning blue
There are strong arguments for pressing blue under different goals or decision frameworks:

- Acausal/superrational coordination: If you expect many agents to reason similarly to you (Hofstadter-style “we all pick the same policy”), choose the policy that yields the best collective outcome when universally adopted. Both “all red” and “all blue” make everyone survive, but blue is more forgiving of partial coordination: if most people pick blue but some deviate, everyone still survives; if most pick red but some deviate, the deviators die. So adopting “press blue” as the shared policy creates a more robust, tolerant equilibrium.

- Altruistic expected value: Even if your single vote is almost never pivotal, there’s a tiny chance it swings the majority. That tiny probability times “billions of lives” can dominate your personal risk. If you place any substantial value on others’ survival, the expected social gain of voting blue can outweigh your personal risk of being on the losing side.

- Social-contract/Schelling-point reasoning: A public norm of “we all press blue” saves everyone even with mild noncompliance, while a norm of “we all press red” makes society brittle—minor disagreements cost lives. Endorsing and acting on the blue norm fosters a safer, higher-trust world.

Bottom line
- Purely self-interested, causal decision theory: press red; it’s a guarantee.
- If you weight others’ lives, or believe your choice is meaningfully correlated with others’ through shared reasoning or norms: there’s a strong case to press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short answer: With private, one-shot choices and no precommitment, expect a red majority. Still, sizable minorities will press blue for coordination or altruistic reasons. Below are realistic clusters and why they lean one way.

Who presses red (survival-dominant, low-trust, or pivotal-skeptic reasoning)
- Risk controllers and adversarial-mindset professionals: security engineers, auditors, actuaries, quantitative traders, poker players. They’re trained to minimize downside when coordination is uncertain; red weakly dominates.
- Caregivers with strong duty to specific dependents: parents of young children, primary caregivers. They prioritize guaranteeing their own survival to keep caring for dependents rather than gamble on a blue majority.
- Classical game-theory/econ thinkers using causal decision theory: many economists, MBAs, competitive strategists. They view blue as adding unnecessary idiosyncratic risk for no personal gain.
- Low-trust, high-cynicism personalities: people who expect widespread defection or confusion. If they predict others will split or lean red, they follow suit.
- People who believe their action is non-pivotal and uncorrelated: “My choice won’t swing billions; if blue wins, I live anyway—so I might as well lock in survival if red wins.”
- Crisis/contingency planners and preppers: trained to assume plans fail and coordination frays under stress; select the policy that survives failure modes.
- Older or more loss-averse individuals: on average more focused on avoiding worst-case personal outcomes; private setting removes social incentives to cooperate.

Who presses blue (coordination-optimistic, altruistic, or superrational reasoning)
- Prosocial frontline workers and humanitarian types: many nurses, doctors, teachers, social workers, NGO staff. They weight others’ survival heavily; the tiny chance of being pivotal times huge social stakes pushes toward blue.
- Rationalist/coordination subcultures: effective altruists, cooperative game theorists, Newcomb/Hofstadter “superrationalists.” They expect correlated reasoning across many minds; choosing blue is the policy they want universally adopted.
- High-trust community members: people embedded in tight, norm-enforcing groups (worker co-ops, intentional communities, well-led teams, some military units). Used to successful coordination and mutual expectations; see blue as the safer collective policy.
- Public-goods cooperators by temperament: individuals who routinely contribute in one-shot dilemmas (as seen in lab studies where a substantial minority cooperates despite a dominant defection option).
- Influenced-by-norms communicators: journalists, educators, civic leaders who believe broad messaging can shift majorities; they anticipate others hearing the same argument and aim to be part of the blue majority.
- Younger idealists and movement joiners: more willing to accept personal risk for a collective win when signaling isn’t required; trust that “most decent people will pick blue.”

What tips the balance
- Privacy: Because choices are private, social signaling and reputation don’t reward blue, pushing more people to red than if choices were public.
- Shared messaging: A clear, credible, widely trusted “everyone press blue” campaign could flip expectations; absent that, default skepticism favors red.
- Perceived correlation: The more people think “others like me will reason as I do,” the more blue gains. The more people think choices are independent noise, the more red dominates.
- Stakes to specific others: People with irreplaceable local responsibilities (dependent care, critical infrastructure roles) skew red; those weighting aggregate lives more heavily skew blue.

Bottom line forecast
- In a sudden, private, one-shot world event with no coordination, expect a red majority driven by risk-dominant, non-pivotal reasoning.
- Expect a sizeable blue minority composed of prosocial, high-trust, and superrational thinkers, and of people convinced that many others will converge on the same cooperative policy.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It depends on what “rational” optimizes—your own survival only, or a broader utility—and on your beliefs about correlation with others’ reasoning.

When blue is irrational
- Pure self-interest + independent choices (classical causal decision theory): Red weakly dominates blue. If blue wins, you live regardless; if red wins, only red lives. So, under this narrow model, pressing blue is irrational.

When blue is rational
- Altruistic utility: If you put any meaningful weight on others’ lives, blue can maximize expected utility. Intuition: there’s a small chance your choice is pivotal (e.g., others are nearly tied). In that case, choosing blue saves billions of people at no cost to your own survival. Back-of-envelope: if the world split is highly uncertain and near 50–50, your pivotal chance scales about 1/√N. With N ≈ 8×10^9, that’s ~10^-5. Then blue is better if you value a random stranger’s life at ≳10^-5 of your own—plausible for many altruists. If you think a red majority is virtually certain, this flips back to red.
- Correlated/superrational reasoning (Hofstadter/functional decision theory): If you expect many agents to adopt the same policy you do because you reason similarly, choosing “press blue” helps instantiate the high-survival equilibrium. Blue is also more robust to imperfect coordination: a blue majority saves everyone, including red deviators; a red majority kills blue deviators.
- Normative/contractarian goals: If you care about which norm society converges on in such dilemmas, adopting and endorsing “press blue” is rational because it yields a safer world under small disagreements.

Bottom line
- Under narrow, self-regarding, uncorrelated beliefs: pressing blue is irrational.
- Under altruistic values, or if you expect meaningful correlation in others’ reasoning, pressing blue is rational—and can be the uniquely rational policy.
